lessonTitle: Pharmacogenetic Variants: CYP2D6, CYP2C19, TPMT and HLA-B*5701

blocks.text: A child recovering from tonsillectomy is given codeine for pain and becomes dangerously drowsy with slow breathing. Codeine is a prodrug that the liver converts to morphine, and in some people a gene duplication makes that conversion unusually fast. A common drug at a normal dose, a hidden genetic difference, and a serious outcome: this is the territory of pharmacogenetics.

blocks.markdown: A **polymorphism** is a genetic variant present in more than about 1% of a population. Pharmacogenetic polymorphisms fall into two broad groups. **Pharmacokinetic** variants alter drug-metabolising enzymes or transporters (for example CYP2D6, CYP2C19, TPMT) and so change drug concentration. **Pharmacodynamic or immune** variants alter targets or immune recognition (for example HLA-B*5701) and so change response or risk of hypersensitivity at normal concentrations.

blocks.title: Metaboliser phenotypes
blocks.text: Genotype is translated into a phenotype by enzyme activity: poor metabolisers (no functional enzyme), intermediate, normal (extensive), and ultra-rapid metabolisers (extra functional gene copies). Effect depends on whether the drug is active itself or a prodrug that needs activation by the enzyme.

blocks.caption: Key pharmacogenetic variants and their clinical consequences.
rows: Codeine, tramadol (prodrugs); metoprolol, tricyclic antidepressants (active drugs)
Prodrugs: poor metabolisers get little effect, ultra-rapid get toxicity. Active drugs: poor metabolisers accumulate drug
Loss-of-function alleles (such as *2 and *3) cause poor metabolism
Clopidogrel (prodrug), omeprazole and other PPIs, citalopram
Clopidogrel: less activation and reduced antiplatelet effect. PPIs: higher exposure
Low or absent activity (homozygous deficiency in about 1 in 300 people)
Accumulation of active thioguanine nucleotides and severe myelosuppression

blocks.title: Predicting the effect of a CYP2D6 variant
blocks.prompt: A patient is a CYP2D6 poor metaboliser. Predict the effect on (a) codeine and (b) metoprolol, a beta-blocker cleared mainly by CYP2D6. (Teaching example.)

steps.text: Identify whether each drug is a prodrug or active. Codeine is a prodrug: CYP2D6 converts it to morphine. Metoprolol is active and is inactivated by CYP2D6.
For codeine, a poor metaboliser forms little morphine, so analgesia is weak and the patient may report that it does not work.
For metoprolol, a poor metaboliser clears the drug slowly, so plasma concentrations are higher at a standard dose, with bradycardia and hypotension more likely.
The same genotype therefore produces opposite effects (reduced benefit versus increased toxicity) depending on whether the drug needs activation or inactivation.

blocks.answer: Codeine: reduced analgesia; metoprolol: accumulation with increased beta-blocker effects.

blocks.markdown: **CYP2C19 and clopidogrel.** Clopidogrel is a prodrug that requires CYP2C19 activation to form the metabolite that blocks the platelet P2Y12 receptor. Poor metabolisers (carriers of two loss-of-function alleles) generate less active metabolite, have reduced platelet inhibition and may have more cardiovascular events after stent placement. An alternative P2Y12 inhibitor can be considered. For omeprazole, poor metabolisers have higher exposure; this is rarely harmful but may explain a stronger effect.

**TPMT and thiopurines.** Azathioprine and mercaptopurine are metabolised partly by thiopurine S-methyltransferase (TPMT). If TPMT activity is low, more drug is converted to active thioguanine nucleotides, which suppress the bone marrow. Testing TPMT activity or genotype before treatment identifies the few homozygous-deficient patients (who should avoid thiopurines or receive a very low dose) and heterozygous patients (about 10%, who usually need a reduced dose). Blood counts must still be monitored in everyone, because other factors also cause marrow suppression.

**HLA-B*5701 and abacavir.** Abacavir, an HIV nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor, can cause a serious multi-system hypersensitivity reaction in carriers of the HLA-B*5701 allele. The drug binds to the HLA-B*5701 protein and changes the peptides it presents, triggering a T-cell immune response. Screening before starting abacavir, and avoiding it in carriers, has greatly reduced hypersensitivity reactions. Patients who test negative have a very low, though not zero, risk and should still be counselled about symptoms.

blocks.caption: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium: q = frequency of a variant allele, p = 1 - q. The frequency of homozygous variant carriers is q squared; heterozygotes 2pq. This assumes random mating and no selection.

blocks.title: How common is TPMT deficiency in carriers?
blocks.prompt: About 1 in 300 people (0.33%) are homozygous for TPMT deficiency. Estimate the allele frequency q and the proportion of heterozygotes. (Assume Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.)

steps.text: Take the square root: q = about 0.058, so p = 1 - 0.058 = 0.942.
Heterozygote frequency = 2pq = 2 x 0.942 x 0.058 = about 0.109, i.e. about 11%.
Interpretation: roughly one in nine people carries one deficient allele and needs a lower thiopurine dose, so testing identifies many more patients than the rare homozygotes.

blocks.answer: q is about 0.058 and about 11% are heterozygous (about 10% in practice)

items: CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 variants change drug exposure; the direction of the clinical effect depends on prodrug versus active drug.
TPMT testing before thiopurines identifies those at risk of myelosuppression; blood counts are still monitored.
HLA-B*5701 screening before abacavir prevents immune-mediated hypersensitivity; carriers should not receive the drug.
Phenotype frequencies differ between ancestry groups, so population context matters.

blocks.title: Prodrug versus active drug
blocks.text: For the same enzyme deficiency, a prodrug loses efficacy (less active metabolite) while an active drug cleared by that enzyme accumulates and causes toxicity. Always ask which kind of drug it is before predicting the effect.

blocks.title: Do not rely on genotype alone
blocks.text: Genotype informs risk but does not replace clinical monitoring such as full blood counts on thiopurines or watching for rash and fever after starting abacavir.

points: CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 polymorphisms alter drug exposure: prodrugs (codeine, clopidogrel) lose efficacy in poor metabolisers, while active drugs accumulate.
TPMT deficiency causes thiopurine accumulation and myelosuppression, so testing guides dose reduction or avoidance.
HLA-B*5701 is an immune variant that predisposes to abacavir hypersensitivity; testing precedes treatment and carriers must not be given the drug.

questions.stem: A CYP2C19 poor metaboliser receives clopidogrel after a coronary stent. What is the expected consequence?

options.text: Reduced conversion to the active metabolite and reduced antiplatelet effect
Increased conversion to the active metabolite and bleeding

questions.correctOptionText: Reduced conversion to the active metabolite and reduced antiplatelet effect

distractorRationale.a: Correct: clopidogrel is a prodrug that requires CYP2C19 activation.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: poor metabolisers form less active drug.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: this relates to HLA variants, not CYP2C19.

questions.explanation: Clopidogrel requires hepatic CYP2C19 to form its active metabolite, so loss-of-function alleles lead to weaker platelet inhibition. An alternative antiplatelet drug may be chosen for such patients.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman who is a CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metaboliser takes tramadol after surgery and becomes drowsy with a respiratory rate of 8 breaths per minute. What explains this?

options.text: Rapid conversion to a more potent opioid metabolite causing higher active drug exposure
Failure to convert tramadol to its active form

questions.correctOptionText: Rapid conversion to a more potent opioid metabolite causing higher active drug exposure

distractorRationale.a: Correct: CYP2D6 forms the active O-desmethyl metabolite, so ultra-rapid metabolisers have excessive opioid effect.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: that would occur in poor metabolisers.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: absorption is not the issue.

questions.explanation: Tramadol is partly activated by CYP2D6, and ultra-rapid metabolisers produce larger amounts of the active metabolite. This can produce opioid toxicity, including respiratory depression, at a normal dose.

questions.stem: A CYP2C19 poor metaboliser is prescribed omeprazole. Compared with normal metabolisers, what is expected?

options.text: No change because omeprazole is not metabolised
Omeprazole is converted to a toxic metabolite

distractorRationale.a: Correct: omeprazole is inactivated by CYP2C19, so slower metabolism raises exposure.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: this would occur in ultra-rapid metabolisers.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: omeprazole is extensively metabolised by CYP2C19.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: no toxic metabolite is implicated.

questions.explanation: Omeprazole is an active drug that is cleared by CYP2C19, so reduced enzyme activity leads to accumulation and a stronger effect. This contrasts with prodrugs such as clopidogrel, where reduced activity lowers effect.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with Crohn disease is about to start azathioprine. Which pre-treatment test is recommended and why?

options.text: TPMT activity or genotype, to identify risk of severe myelosuppression

questions.correctOptionText: TPMT activity or genotype, to identify risk of severe myelosuppression

distractorRationale.a: Correct: low TPMT leads to accumulation of toxic thiopurine nucleotides.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: HLA-B*5701 is relevant to abacavir.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: CYP2D6 is unrelated to azathioprine metabolism.

questions.explanation: TPMT inactivates thiopurines, so deficiency leads to excess active thioguanine nucleotides and bone marrow failure. Pre-treatment testing allows dose reduction or avoidance.

questions.stem: A loss-of-function allele of a drug-metabolising enzyme has an allele frequency of 0.2 in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. What percentage of people are homozygous for the allele (and so are poor metabolisers)?
questions.explanation: Homozygous frequency = q squared = 0.2 x 0.2 = 0.04, which is 4%. Under Hardy-Weinberg, random mating and no selection are assumed.

questions.stem: A deficient-activity allele has a frequency of 0.1 in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. What percentage of people are heterozygous carriers (intermediate metabolisers)?
questions.explanation: With q = 0.1 and p = 0.9, heterozygote frequency = 2pq = 2 x 0.9 x 0.1 = 0.18, i.e. 18%. Heterozygotes are far more numerous than homozygotes (1%), which is why testing identifies many patients needing dose reduction.

questions.stem: Describe the role of TPMT testing before thiopurine therapy and how the result is used.
markingGuide: TPMT inactivates thiopurines (azathioprine, mercaptopurine) by methylation
Low activity causes accumulation of active thioguanine nucleotides and severe myelosuppression
Homozygous deficiency (about 1 in 300): avoid or use markedly reduced dose
Normal activity: standard dosing but full blood counts and liver tests still monitored because other causes of toxicity exist
questions.explanation: Testing converts a hidden risk of severe marrow suppression into a dosing decision before treatment begins. Monitoring continues because TPMT status explains only part of thiopurine toxicity.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with HIV is being considered for an abacavir-containing regimen. His HLA-B*5701 test is positive. What is the appropriate management?

options.text: Do not prescribe abacavir and record the result as a hypersensitivity risk
Prescribe abacavir and check the full blood count weekly

questions.correctOptionText: Do not prescribe abacavir and record the result as a hypersensitivity risk

distractorRationale.a: Correct: carriers are at high risk of a serious hypersensitivity reaction.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: the reaction is immune mediated and not dose-related.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: an antihistamine does not prevent the reaction.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: blood count monitoring is not the relevant safeguard.

questions.explanation: HLA-B*5701 presents abacavir-modified peptides to T cells, triggering a potentially fatal immune reaction at normal doses. The drug is therefore avoided in carriers.

questions.stem: Explain why HLA-B*5701 testing precedes abacavir treatment and what a negative result does and does not mean.
markingGuide: HLA-B*5701 is an immune gene variant (HLA class I), not a metabolic enzyme
Abacavir interacts with the HLA-B*5701 protein and alters the peptides presented, activating T cells
Result is a serious multi-system hypersensitivity reaction (fever, rash, gastrointestinal and respiratory symptoms) that can be fatal on rechallenge
Testing before treatment and avoiding the drug in carriers prevents reactions
Negative result greatly lowers but does not abolish risk, so patients are still counselled about symptoms and told to stop and seek help
questions.explanation: The reaction is immune mediated, so testing for the responsible allele allows it to be prevented rather than treated. A negative test lowers risk but cannot exclude all hypersensitivity.

questions.stem: Explain how polymorphisms in CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 alter drug response, distinguishing the effect on a prodrug from the effect on an active drug.
markingGuide: Polymorphisms change enzyme activity: poor, intermediate, normal and ultra-rapid metabolisers
Prodrug requiring activation: poor metaboliser forms less active drug (e.g. codeine via CYP2D6, clopidogrel via CYP2C19) so reduced efficacy
Prodrug in ultra-rapid metaboliser: excess active metabolite and toxicity (e.g. codeine or tramadol)
Active drug inactivated by the enzyme: poor metaboliser accumulates drug (e.g. metoprolol via CYP2D6, omeprazole via CYP2C19)
Clinical use: genotype can guide drug choice or dose
questions.explanation: The same enzyme change gives opposite effects depending on whether the enzyme activates or inactivates the drug. This is why identifying the drug type is essential before predicting the clinical consequence.
